results.title: The WHO-5 well-being index – validation based on item response theory and the analysis of measurement invariance across 35 countries - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Research Paper The WHO-5 well-being index – validation based on item response theory and the analysis of measurement invariance across 35 countries. The WHO-5 showed some non-invariant parameters across countries. Large-scale cross-cultural studies that use the WHO-5 should employ a latent variable modeling approach that accounts for non-invariant parameter across countries. Despite its frequent use, some psychometric questions remain that concern the choice of an adequate item response theory (IRT) model, the evaluation of reliability at important cutoff points, and most importantly the assessment of measurement invariance across countries. An in-depth IRT analysis was conducted for each country, testing different IRT assumptions (e.g., unidimensionality), comparing different IRT-models, and calculating reliabilities. Furthermore, measurement invariance analysis was conducted with the recently proposed alignment procedure. Measurement invariance analysis revealed metric invariance but discarded scalar invariance across countries. However, large-scale cross-cultural studies should employ a latent variable modeling approach that accounts for non-invariant parameters across countries (e.g., alignment).

results.title: How I Conducted Measurement Invariance in PLS-SEM Using ...
results.content: Published Time: 2025-04-01T05:13:00.425Z How I Conducted Measurement Invariance in PLS-SEM Using SmartPLS 4.0 Photo by Andrew Moca on Unsplash I still remember the first time I tried to compare consumer behavior across different groups in my research. Simply put, MI ensures that a construct (like brand authenticity) is measured equivalently across different groups. Why Measurement Invariance is a Big Deal Imagine I’m comparing brand loyalty between two groups: Millennials and Baby Boomers. If my construct is measured differently across groups, then any observed differences might be due to the way people interpret the questions, rather than real behavioral differences. That’s why I now make MI testing a standard step whenever I conduct multi-group analyses in PLS-SEM. If I don’t test for MI, I can’t be sure whether changes in trust scores reflect real attitude shifts or just differences in how consumers interpret survey questions over time. MI also applies in experimental studies, where I need to ensure that my control and treatment groups perceive my constructs the same way before I compare outcomes. How I Conducted Measurement Invariance in SmartPLS 4.0 Once I understood why MI was so important, I needed to test it in my own research. **Step 2: Compositional Invariance – Are My Latent Variable Scores Comparable?** Next, I had to test whether my composite scores were calculated the same way across groups. That meant my measurement was fully invariant across income levels, and I could confidently compare my model results across groups. A Hypothetical Example: How Measurement Invariance Can Change Findings Let’s say I’m studying the effect of social media influencers on purchase intention in two groups: Gen Z and Millennials. By testing MI in SmartPLS 4.0, I ensure that my constructs are truly comparable. But if MI doesn’t hold, I know my groups interpret purchase intention differently, and I need to refine my measurement model. Now, every time I conduct multi-group research, testing for MI is non-negotiable. By following three steps – configural invariance, compositional invariance, and equality of means/variances – I can confidently compare my model results across different groups.
